Ivory
EYE-vuh-ree
noun
Through the Old French ivurie from the Latin ebur, elephant tooth — the hard white substance of the tusk, brought to Israel by the navy of Tharshish and prized above almost every material for its whiteness and its cost.

Biblical Definition

Ivory is the dense white substance of the elephant’s tusk, imported into Israel by sea and reckoned among the costliest of materials. Scripture uses it two ways, and they stand at opposite ends of the moral world. In the Song and the Psalms it is beauty: the beloved’s body as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires, the bride’s neck as a tower of ivory, and the King’s garments smelling of myrrh and aloes and cassia “out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad” (Psa 45:8) — a messianic psalm, where the ivory is the splendour of the Bridegroom’s own house. Solomon’s great throne of ivory overlaid with the best gold belongs here too, the glory of a kingdom at peace. But ivory turns. Ahab built an ivory house (1Ki 22:39), and the historian sets that single fact beside a reign of Baal-worship and Naboth’s stolen vineyard, so that the panelling and the murder stand in one sentence. Amos then pronounces sentence: “the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall have an end, saith the LORD” (Amo 3:15). His indictment is not luxury alone but luxury asleep — men who “lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches” while the ruin of Joseph goes unlamented (Amo 6:4-6).

Webster 1828 Definition

The hard white substance of the elephant’s tusk; in Scripture the splendour of Solomon’s throne and the Bridegroom’s palaces, and the emblem of Samaria’s luxury under judgment.

expand to see more

IVORY, n. [Fr. ivoire; L. ebur, the tooth of an elephant.] The tusk of the elephant, a hard, solid, firm substance, of a fine white colour, susceptible of a high polish.

It was brought to Palestine by the navy of Tharshish, with gold, silver, apes, and peacocks (1Ki 10:22).

Used for thrones, beds, couches, panelling, benches, and vessels (1Ki 10:18; Amo 6:4; Eze 27:6; Rev 18:12).

An ivory house is one wainscotted or inlaid with ivory, as Ahab’s (1Ki 22:39) and those of Samaria (Amo 3:15).

Figuratively, whiteness and smoothness of surpassing beauty (Son 5:14; 7:4).

Key Scripture

1Ki 22:39 — "Now the rest of the acts of Ahab, and all that he did, and the ivory house which he made, and all the cities that he built, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?"

Amo 3:15 — "And I will smite the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall have an end, saith the LORD."

Amo 6:4 — "That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;"

Psa 45:8 — "All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia, out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad."

Modern Corruption

Amos is quoted selectively at both extremes — enlisted as a manifesto against wealth as such, or dismissed by the comfortable as thundering about somebody else’s beds.

expand to see more

Amo 6:4 is a favourite text of preaching that treats prosperity itself as the crime, and on that reading Solomon’s ivory throne would be a sin and Psa 45’s ivory palaces a scandal. Amos says something more searching. Read the sentence to its end: they lie upon beds of ivory, they chant to the sound of the viol, they drink wine in bowls and anoint themselves with the chief ointments, “but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.” That last clause is the indictment. The sin is a couch so comfortable that the nation’s ruin cannot reach the man lying on it — wealth used as an anaesthetic against the things that ought to have broken his heart. The opposite error is just as common, and it belongs to those who are comfortable: Amos is read as a period piece about eighth-century Samaria, or as a rebuke aimed at somebody richer, always somebody richer, and so the couch stays exactly where it is.

Ahab’s house makes the same point in narrative. The chronicler mentions the ivory house in one breath with the record of a reign, and the reader who knows the previous chapters knows what stood in the walls: Jezebel’s prophets fed at the queen’s table, the vineyard of a murdered man, a kingdom taught to worship Baal. Ivory panelling is not sin; ivory panelling paid for by Naboth’s blood, in a house that hunted Elijah, is the exact shape of what God overthrows. Amos promises that the winter house and the summer house go down together, and Revelation closes the account, listing vessels of ivory in the cargo of a city that falls in a single hour. So the word puts one question to a comfortable man, and it is not how much do you own but what can still reach you. If the affliction of Joseph can no longer get through the panelling, the panelling is already under sentence.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The white tusk of the elephant — Solomon’s throne and the Bridegroom’s palaces on one hand, Ahab’s house and Samaria’s couches on the other.

expand to see more

Ivory — Old French ivurie, Latin ebur, the elephant’s tooth.

Hebrew shen, a tooth, alone or with habbim (elephants) in 1Ki 10:22.

Imported by the navy of Tharshish once in three years with gold, apes, and peacocks.

Ahab’s ivory house (1Ki 22:39) stands in the record beside Baal and Naboth’s vineyard.

Amo 3:15 and 6:4 sentence the ivory houses and the ivory beds; Rev 18:12 lists ivory in Babylon’s last cargo.

Usage

"Psa 45:8 puts ivory palaces around the Bridegroom — the material itself is never the sin."

"Amos condemns the couch that made a man unable to grieve for the affliction of Joseph."

"The chronicler names Ahab’s ivory house and Naboth’s vineyard in the same record for a reason."
